title: The Bank changes who bears clearing losses and when members can see margin demands
summary: The Bank of England’s near-final CCP rulebook makes two connected choices about stress in cleared markets. Members and clients should have more information about the collateral they may have to raise. The clearing house itself should also have capital at risk alongside the members whose resources can be used after a default. Nineteen parties responded to the earlier consultation. The Bank reports broad support for putting the firm-facing parts of UK EMIR into a clearer domestic rulebook, alongside differences between clearing houses, members and clients on how the costs and risks should be shared. The November statement sets out the revisions and the dates on which firms should prepare to implement them.

The new second tranche of clearing-house capital illustrates why the amount and the order of losses must be read together. The consultation proposed 25% of the CCP’s risk-weighted capital requirement. The near-final rule sets 10%, with the resources used alongside the mutualised default fund of non-defaulting members. Placing capital there makes it more likely to absorb losses than placing it after the entire fund has been depleted. The Bank judged that a smaller amount could therefore still strengthen incentives for default management. The percentage is measured against the CCP’s capital requirement, not against the total default fund or the losses that a particular member could incur. The new deadline for meeting the requirement is 1 April 2028.

Margin transparency addresses a different stage of the same stress. The Bank wants clients to have access to margin simulators when they request access and it is feasible to provide it, and to receive a forward-looking indication across relevant stress scenarios. Only material add-ons need to be included in simulators. Public descriptions can explain the model components that drive responsiveness at a high level. The Bank extended the simulator implementation period to 24 months after the rules come into force, and allowed 12 months for assessing procyclicality and certain other transparency requirements. A modelled call can inform a liquidity buffer, but the statement gives no assurance that the realised call will match the simulation.

The rules on moving client positions after a clearing-member default also changed. The Bank dropped its proposal to make the allocation of default fund contributions depend on client portability. The detail for omnibus accounts recognises the operational difficulty when clients have not designated the same replacement member. For clients, a formal ability to transfer positions is different from having a receiving member and the information needed to complete a transfer under stress. Meanwhile, changes to supervisory processes include clearer notification requirements and a route for limited introduction of new collateral. The diagram in the innovation chapter distinguishes notification from additional permission when collateral is ineligible or introduces material risks.

The package remained near-final while Treasury legislation was outstanding. The Bank expected commencement by the end of the first quarter of 2027, with at least three months for implementation of most provisions and the longer periods for specified changes. Annexes include the draft instruments and a transposition table mapping requirements. A separate, narrower consultation in this publication concerned revoking the existing operational incident reporting rule when replacement reporting requirements were due to start on 18 March 2027. Its response deadline, 30 November, did not reopen the entire CCP rulebook.

questions.question: How much loss could reach a particular member alongside the CCP’s new capital tranche?
questions.detail: The near-final 10% uses the CCP’s risk-weighted capital requirement as its denominator. A clearing member needs its own default fund share and the position of every resource in the relevant service’s waterfall to estimate an exposure. Reconstruct the waterfall from the CCP’s disclosures and rules, then apply common stressed losses to both the proposed and previous structures. The calibration alone cannot establish the change in the member’s loss.

questions.question: Would the new margin information materially change a client’s liquidity buffer?
questions.detail: Simulators need only capture material add-ons, and the forward-looking output depends on the scenarios considered. A client could face demands from more than one clearing service in the same episode. Obtain the actual simulator coverage, stress assumptions and access arrangements from each clearing provider. Compare modelled calls with the client’s portfolio and collateral availability, including timing differences before treating an estimated peak as a funding requirement.

questions.question: Could a client’s positions actually move to its preferred replacement member during a default?
questions.detail: The consultation response modifies the approach to omnibus accounts and drops the proposed link between portability and default fund allocation. For a client, the alternative to successful transfer could involve closing or replacing positions. Review the account structure, designation of a receiving clearing member, agreements and operational tests. Check whether the receiving member can accept the portfolio and collateral under the conditions of the default scenario.

limitation: The statement and associated instruments were near-final on 16 November. Expected commencement, exemption decisions and eventual realised losses are distinct from the policy choices described.
